Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish' directly conflicts with 'I can talk about what happened very easily.' These items describe opposing levels of verbal access to the trauma memory and are hard to reconcile as the same patient's current self-report.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with marked memory disturbance items ('some moments are extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'there are parts of the event I simply cannot remember'). Although fragmented trauma memory can coexist with disclosure, the wording 'very easily' is hard to reconcile with this level of fragmentation in the same profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
issues.explanation: Across Memory and Negative Appraisals, reporting that one can talk about the event 'very easily' sits in tension with the appraisal 'If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it.' Patients may force themselves to discuss trauma despite distress, but these two statements point in opposite directions and are difficult to integrate clinically without additional context.

vignette: John, a 63-year-old community organizer of Oceania descent, has been living with the haunting aftermath of a life-threatening accident that occurred several years ago. The event itself is still vividly etched in his mind, yet certain parts remain shrouded in an impenetrable fog. John describes specific moments with crystal clarity—the piercing scream of brakes, the smell of burning rubber—but other critical details are lost to him entirely. Despite his efforts to piece together what happened, he often finds himself unable to articulate it fully. John's triggers have become increasingly prevalent and intrusive since the accident. The mere sight of military or police uniforms sets off a visceral reaction that leaves him feeling as if he were still in danger. He is especially sensitive to others expressing anger, even calmly, which sends him into a state of heightened anxiety. Each trigger serves as a painful reminder of his own feelings of numbness and self-blame, reinforcing the belief that he somehow played a role in what transpired. His negative appraisals have significantly impacted how he processes memories of the event. John often feels emotionally numbed, almost as if he is watching the events unfold from afar rather than experiencing them directly. This detachment exacerbates his memory gaps and confusion, making it even harder to reconstruct the full narrative of the accident. He has come to believe that his body's automatic responses—such as increased heart rate and sweating—are further evidence of his inadequacy and self-inflicted harm. The cycle perpetuates itself; John’s heightened emotional numbness and feelings of self-blame exacerbate his triggers, making them more intense and frequent. This, in turn, deepens his negative appraisals and distorts how he remembers the event. He finds himself avoiding situations that might trigger these overwhelming sensations, isolating himself from community events where uniformed personnel are often present. John’s occupation as a community organizer has also been affected by this cycle. His aversion to confrontation and his tendency to avoid conflict mean that he now shies away from important meetings or discussions that involve heated debates. This has strained relationships with colleagues who rely on him for leadership during challenging times. John knows that these avoidance behaviors have consequences, but the fear of triggering another overwhelming episode keeps him locked in a cycle of self-imposed isolation. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that his daily life was becoming increasingly unmanageable. He feared losing the sense of purpose he once found in his work and worried about the long-term effects on his relationships with friends and family. Despite his fears, he is also hopeful that therapy might provide a way to regain some control over his life and find a path toward healing. Through John’s journey, it becomes clear how each element—triggers, memory difficulties, and negative appraisals—are intertwined in a complex web of reactions and beliefs that perpetuate his distress. The clarity and intensity of certain memories contrast sharply with the gaps and confusion others leave behind, reinforcing his sense of helplessness and self-blame. It is within this cycle that John seeks support to navigate the challenges he faces and reclaim a more fulfilling life.
